idiom_name: value-receiver methods returning the value type (func (m Money) Add(n Money) Money)
implementation_notes: Go has no operator overloading, so closure is written by hand as an ordinary method with a value receiver that returns a new value of the same type; because the receiver is copied, such a method cannot alias the operand, which is exactly the value semantics the pattern assumes. What replaces the classic structure is that convention plus unexported fields and a constructor that validates, so each method rebuilds the value from the canonical representation. The standard library shows a deliberately opposite convention - math/big's func (z *Int) Add(x, y *Int) *Int writes the result into the receiver and returns it for chaining, trading the arithmetic reading for allocation control - and that shape should stay in numeric hot paths, not in domain values; use it only when profiling shows the per-operation allocation matters.
pitfalls: A pointer receiver turns the closed signature into mutation: func (m *Money) Add(n Money) Money changes the operand, so m.Add(n) is no longer a combination; pick value receivers for domain values and reserve pointer receivers for documented in-place accumulators.
Value receivers copy the whole struct on every call; keep the type small (or return pointer-free structs of a few words) if combinations happen in loops.

With unexported fields the zero value is invalid, so folds need an explicit identity (Zero(cur)) - and interfaces cannot express 'supports +', so polymorphic combination must be declared as an interface method returning the type itself.
